item.title: “Monks, suppose the Ganges river carries along a great pile of foam. A person with good eyesight would look at it, reflect, and examine it.…
item.description:
“Monks, suppose the Ganges river carries along a great pile of foam. A person with good eyesight would look at it, reflect, and examine it. Looking, reflecting, examining, the foam would appear empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a pile of foam? So too, monks, whatever form there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near — a monk sees form, reflects, examines it. Seeing, reflecting, examining, form appears empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be in form?”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.95
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Here, monks, a well-taught noble disciple reflects: ‘Now I am being overwhelmed by form. In the past, I was also overwhelmed by form just as…
item.description:
“Here, monks, a well-taught noble disciple reflects: ‘Now I am being overwhelmed by form. In the past, I was also overwhelmed by form just as I am now being overwhelmed by present form. If I were to delight in future form, then in the future I would be overwhelmed by form just as I am now being overwhelmed by present form.’ Reflecting thus, he has no regret for past form, no delight in future form, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.79
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “That is so, great king. Few are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, do not become infatuated, do not become intoxicated,…
item.description:
“That is so, great king. Few are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, do not become infatuated, do not become intoxicated, do not fall into heedlessness regarding sensual pleasures, and do not act wrongly toward others. But many are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, become infatuated, intoxicated, fall into heedlessness regarding sensual pleasures, and act wrongly toward others.

Bemused by wealth and sensual pleasures,
People are greedy and deluded,
In the midst of sensual pleasures,
Without clear awareness,
They are overly intoxicated,
Like a deer unaware of the trap set —
Later they suffer,
Experiencing the results of evil deeds.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.6
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I will dwell…
item.description:
“Good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I will dwell alone, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute.” - “Koṭṭhita, whatever is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. And what, Koṭṭhita, is suffering? The eye is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Forms are suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Eye-consciousness is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Eye-contact is suffering — there you should abandon your desire. Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact — pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant — that feeling is suffering. There you should abandon your desire.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.163
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Māgandiya, suppose a leprous person with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails,…
item.description:
“Māgandiya, suppose a leprous person with sores and blisters on his limbs, being devoured by worms, scratching the openings of his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a charcoal pit. The more he scratches the wound openings and cauterizes his body, the more those wound openings become impure, foul-smelling, and infected, yet he feels some ease and satisfaction because of the itching of the wound openings. So too, Māgandiya, beings who have not abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures. The more they indulge in sensual pleasures, the more their craving for sensual pleasures increases, and the more they are burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, yet they feel some ease and satisfaction dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 75 – Māgandiyasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Venerable Jatukaṇṇī: “Having heard of the hero, free from desire for sensual pleasures, I have come to ask the desireless one, Who has crossed the…
item.description:
Venerable Jatukaṇṇī:
“Having heard of the hero, free from desire for sensual pleasures,
I have come to ask the desireless one,
Who has crossed the flood,
The one born with the eye —
Speak the path of peace,
Let the Blessed One tell it to me as it is.

Having conquered sensual desires,
The Blessed One lives in the world
Like the sun illuminating the earth with its radiance.
O great wise one, teach me the Dhamma —
I am of little wisdom —
That by knowing it, I might overcome birth and old age.”

The Blessed One replied to Jatukaṇṇī:
“Subdue greed for sensual pleasures,
See renunciation as peace.
Do not hold on to or reject anything in the world.

Dry up what has gone before,
Let there be nothing after —
If you grasp nothing in the middle,
You will live at peace.

For one who has no ‘mine’ at all
In name-and-form, O brahmin,
There are no defilements by which
One would be in death’s power.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 5.12
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And what, monks, are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness, unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind; ill-will is a defilement of the mind;…
item.description:
“And what, monks, are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness, unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind; ill-will is a defilement of the mind; anger is a defilement of the mind; hostility is a defilement of the mind; hypocrisy, spite, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, vanity, heedlessness are defilements of the mind.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 7 – Vatthūpamasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise them,…
item.description:
“Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then delight ceases. Migajāla, I say that with the cessation of delight, suffering ceases. Sounds … Odors … Tastes … Touches … Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind … If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then delight ceases. Migajāla, I say that with the cessation of delight, suffering ceases.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.64
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: The Blessed One replied to Upasīva: “Mindful, not longing for anything, You will cross the flood. Abandoning sensual desires, free from doubt, Day and night…
item.description:
The Blessed One replied to Upasīva:
“Mindful, not longing for anything,
You will cross the flood.
Abandoning sensual desires, free from doubt,
Day and night see clearly —
The destruction of craving is Nibbāna.”

“One who is completely dispassionate
Toward all sensual pleasures,
Depending on nothing, giving up all else —
Freed completely, that is the supreme liberation.
There, that one abides,
And does not go on.”

“Just as a flame blown by strong wind
Goes to its end and cannot be measured,
So too the sage, freed from name and body,
Goes to his end and cannot be measured.”

“For one who has reached the end,
There is no measure by which one could speak of him.
When all phenomena are uprooted,
All paths of speech are uprooted as well.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 5.7
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: The inner fetter and the outer fetter — Beings are entangled in these fetters. I ask Gotama about this — Who can escape these fetters?…
item.description:
The inner fetter and the outer fetter —
Beings are entangled in these fetters.
I ask Gotama about this —
Who can escape these fetters?

(The Blessed One)
A person established in virtue, wise,
Developing mind and wisdom,
Ardent and discreet —
That monk can escape the fetters.
One who has abandoned greed,
Hatred, and ignorance,
The defilement-free arahant —
He has escaped the fetters.
Where name-and-form is destroyed
Without remainder,
Where the hindrance and perceptions of form are destroyed —
There the fetters are cut.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 7.6
